claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native surface oxide formed during processing.
The native oxide on Q235 steel effectively limits corrosion during room-temperature aggressive-salt exposure.
At room temperature, the oxide acts as a compact passive barrier that impedes ingress of aggressive ions.
Ion diffusion is minimal during room-temperature salt exposure, allowing the native oxide to remain intact.
Exposure at 700–900 °C accelerates elemental diffusion in the alloy and scale.
High-temperature salt exposure causes loss, reaction, or redistribution of Mn and Si in Q235 steel.
Mn and Si are crucial for forming a compact, protective oxide on Q235 steel.
Accelerated diffusion and loss of protective elements structurally compromise the Q235 oxide scale at 700–900 °C.
The compromised high-temperature oxide deteriorates or spalls, opening paths for rapid corrosion attack.
Room-temperature-exposed Q235 steel will have a low corrosion rate and a continuous, minimally altered oxide layer.
At room temperature, Q235 corrosion behavior will be similar to that of a reference material having a stable oxide.
High-temperature salt exposure will produce significantly greater mass loss than room-temperature exposure.
High-temperature salt exposure will produce oxide spallation, discontinuity, and elemental depletion in Q235 steel.
Pre-annealing may form a more thermally stable oxide and retain corrosion protection.
A significant pre-treatment such as controlled annealing may make the proposed mechanism inapplicable.
The mechanism may not apply when salt composition or environmental conditions differ substantially from Na2SO4/NaCl exposure at 700–900 °C.
The respective contributions of Mn and Si to oxide integrity are uncertain.
The detailed kinetics of oxide breakdown under high-temperature salt exposure are uncertain.
